That doesn't refute what I said. They were referred to as microcomputers and it wasn't until the IBM PC really popularised the name and it became used to describe a computer that was compatible that PC really became the standard term rather than calling them micros. Of course, all micros were by definition personal computers, heck I remember buying Personal Computer World magazine as far back as 1980, and yet these personal computers were still always referred to as microcomputers or micros. PC was largely associated with the particular style of computer initially offered by IBM and later cloned by Compaq and others which were intended for the office and small business market. Earliest use doesn't change that, the term wasn't commonly used for computers regular people bought until the 1990 when the traditional home microcomputer was superseded by the IBM PC compatibles and to indicate the difference from the older micros, people switched to using the term PC. Before that, if you asked someone what computer they had they would say 'Amiga', 'ST', 'Archimedes' and so on and there was no expectation of compatibility between them. The use of PC also implied that the software was PC compatible and that's why you wouldn't describe an Amiga as a PC despite it clearly being a personal computer. Once all the other non-PC compatibles had been driven out of the market by 1990-1995 and the market standardised on Windows (I personally went from my BBC Micro to a 486 running Linux in 1995) then the concept of going to buy a 'PC' became the norm as they would all run the same software and the IBM PC Compatible bit was lost. This is all history. It doesn't change the fact that all these single use microcomputers were personal computers, just that the PC term wasn't used to describe them. They were described by their brand or generically just as micro. Today, there's a bit of a backlash against the fact that PC was used to describe a machine running Windows but we got there through a logical process. We could call it a Windows PC to be more precise but people won't do that, they just still think of PC as being that compatible box.

TL:DR - They were personal computers, they were referred to as personal computers, there was Personal Computer World magazine, but because Wintel co-opted the term we retroactively say that they weren't called Personal Computers even when they were. :P
